claim: Thy1-αSyn mice overexpress wild-type human α-synuclein
source: In mice overexpressing the human amyloid α-synuclein (αSyn), we reveal that colonization with curli-producing Escherichia coli promotes αSyn pathology in the gut and the brain.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the mice overexpress human α-synuclein in the abstract.

claim: Colonization with curli-producing Escherichia coli promotes αSyn pathology in the gut and brain of Thy1-αSyn mice
source: In mice overexpressing the human amyloid α-synuclein (αSyn), we reveal that colonization with curli-producing Escherichia coli promotes αSyn pathology in the gut and the brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Curli expression is required for E. coli to exacerbate αSyn-induced behavioral deficits
source: Curli expression is required for E. coli to exacerbate αSyn-induced behavioral deficits, including intestinal and motor impairments.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by comparison experiments with curli-deficient mutants.

claim: Purified curli subunits accelerate αSyn aggregation in biochemical assays
source: Purified curli subunits accelerate αSyn aggregation in biochemical assays, while oral treatment of mice with a gut-restricted amyloid inhibitor prevents curli-mediated acceleration of pathology and behavioral abnormalities.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro aggregation assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Oral treatment with a gut-restricted amyloid inhibitor prevents curli-mediated acceleration of pathology and behavioral abnormalities
source: Purified curli subunits accelerate αSyn aggregation in biochemical assays, while oral treatment of mice with a gut-restricted amyloid inhibitor prevents curli-mediated acceleration of pathology and behavioral abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by EGCG treatment experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Exposure to microbial amyloids in the gastrointestinal tract can accelerate αSyn aggregation and disease in the gut and brain
source: We propose that exposure to microbial amyloids in the gastrointestinal tract can accelerate αSyn aggregation and disease in the gut and the brain.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Synucleinopathies include Parkinson's disease, Lewy Body disease, and Multiple System Atrophy
source: Synucleinopathies are one family of amyloid disease, which includes Parkinson's disease (PD), Lewy Body disease (LBD), and Multiple System Atrophy (MSA).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Accumulation of α-Synuclein into insoluble amyloid aggregations leads to inflammation and neuronal dysfunction
source: Central to their pathogenesis is the accumulation of the neuronal protein α-Synuclein (αSyn) into insoluble amyloid aggregations, which ultimately leads to inflammation and neuronal dysfunction (Jucker and Walker, 2013; Brettschneider et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: αSyn aggregation can contribute to the death of dopaminergic neurons in specific brain regions, resulting in motor symptoms
source: αSyn aggregation can contribute to the death of dopaminergic neurons in specific brain regions, resulting in motor symptoms (Poewe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Accumulation of αSyn aggregates may first occur at peripheral sites such as the olfactory epithelium or gastrointestinal tract before spreading to the brain
source: Clinical and epidemiological data suggest that accumulation of αSyn aggregates may first occur at peripheral sites, such as the olfactory epithelium or gastrointestinal (GI) tract, before spreading to the brain (Braak et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior clinical and epidemiological data.

claim: Individuals with synucleinopathies often display constipation and GI dysfunctions years prior to movement dysfunction onset
source: Individuals diagnosed with various synucleinopathies often display constipation and other GI dysfunctions years prior to the onset of movement dysfunction (Verbaan et al., 2007; Colosimo, 2011; Engen et al., 2017; Mertsalmi et al., 2017; Sakakibara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Experimental evidence exists for prion-like spread of αSyn aggregates
source: Experimental evidence exists for a prion-like spread of αSyn aggregates (Woerman et al., 2015), including propagation from the gut to the brain via the vagus nerve and/or spinal cord in rodent models (Holmqvist et al., 2014; Uemura et al., 2018; Van Den Berge et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Truncal vagotomy is associated with decreased risk of Parkinson's disease in humans
source: In humans, recent epidemiological studies suggest an association between truncal vagotomy and appendectomy with a decreased risk of PD (Svensson et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Killinger et al., 2018), and in increased risk of comorbidity with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (Hui et al., 2018; Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Inflammatory bowel disease is associated with increased risk of Parkinson's disease comorbidity
source: In humans, recent epidemiological studies suggest an association between truncal vagotomy and appendectomy with a decreased risk of PD (Svensson et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Killinger et al., 2018), and in increased risk of comorbidity with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) (Hui et al., 2018; Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: The gut microbiome impacts development and function of the immune, metabolic and nervous systems
source: The gut is colonized with a complex microbiome that impacts development and function of the immune, metabolic and nervous systems (Fung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Enterobacteriaceae can produce functional amyloid proteins termed curli
source: Enterobacteriaceae, highly prevalent within the gut of humans, can produce functional amyloid proteins termed curli (Tursi and Tükel, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Curli fibers are formed by bacterial secretion of unfolded CsgA that aggregates extracellularly
source: Curli fibers are formed by bacterial secretion of an unfolded amyloid, CsgA, that subsequently aggregates extracellularly to form biofilms, mediate adhesion to epithelial cells, and are involved in bacteriophage defense (Tursi and Tükel, 2018; Vidakovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Exposure to curli modulates host inflammatory responses within the intestinal tract and periphery
source: Exposure to curli not only modulates host inflammatory responses within the intestinal tract and periphery (Gallo et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Tursi and Tükel, 2018), but oral administration of curli-producing bacteria can also increase production and aggregation of the amyloid protein αSyn in aged rats and nematodes (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Oral administration of curli-producing bacteria increases production and aggregation of αSyn in aged rats and nematodes
source: Exposure to curli not only modulates host inflammatory responses within the intestinal tract and periphery (Gallo et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Tursi and Tükel, 2018), but oral administration of curli-producing bacteria can also increase production and aggregation of the amyloid protein αSyn in aged rats and nematodes (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Native bacterial chaperones of curli can transiently interact with αSyn and modulate its aggregation
source: Biochemical studies demonstrate that native, bacterial chaperones of curli are capable of transiently interacting with αSyn and modulating its aggregation (Chorell et al., 2015; Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: Diverse human amyloid proteins including αSyn, Aβ, PrPC, and Tau can accelerate amyloidogenesis of heterologous mammalian amyloid proteins
source: Interestingly, diverse human amyloid proteins including αSyn, amyloid beta (Aβ), cellular prion protein (PrPC), and Tau can accelerate the amyloidogenesis of heterologous mammalian amyloid proteins (Clinton et al., 2010; Brettschneider et al., 2015; Katorcha et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Lesions containing mixed human amyloids have been observed in neurodegenerative brains
source: Lesions containing mixed human amyloids have been observed in neurodegenerative brains (Rahimi and Kovacs, 2014; Spires-Jones et al., 2017), implicating interactions between different amyloidogenic proteins in resulting pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior observations.

claim: Depletion of the microbiome reduces pathophysiology in Thy1-αSyn mice
source: We previously identified that depletion of the microbiome reduces pathophysiology in Thy1-αSyn mice (alpha-synuclein overexpressing; ASO mice) (Sampson et al., 2016), which overexpress wild-type human αSyn.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Thy1-αSyn mice display increased neuroinflammation, GI dysfunction, and progressive motor abnormalities due to accumulation and aggregation of neuronal αSyn
source: Due to accumulation and aggregation of neuronal αSyn, mice display increased neuroinflammation, GI dysfunction, and progressive motor abnormalities (Rockenstein et al., 2002; Chesselet et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012) that are relevant in the study of synucleinopathies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior characterizations of the mouse model.

claim: Increased colonization and mucosal association with Enterobacteriaceae have been reported in individuals with Parkinson's disease compared to healthy controls
source: Interestingly, increased colonization and mucosal association with Enterobacteriaceae, such as E. coli, have been reported in individuals with PD compared to healthy controls (Forsyth et al., 2011), as well as a positive association of Enterobacteriaceae abundance with disease severity (Scheperjans et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Enterobacteriaceae abundance is positively associated with Parkinson's disease severity
source: Interestingly, increased colonization and mucosal association with Enterobacteriaceae, such as E. coli, have been reported in individuals with PD compared to healthy controls (Forsyth et al., 2011), as well as a positive association of Enterobacteriaceae abundance with disease severity (Scheperjans et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: E. coli exacerbated αSyn-dependent motor defects in ASO animals compared to B. fragilis and SFB
source: E. coli exacerbated the αSyn-dependent motor defects in ASO animals across a battery of tests, compared to the other taxa (Figure 1A–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Colonization with curli-deficient E. coli did not elicit robust motor impairment in ASO mice
source: Evaluation of coordinated motor function revealed that colonization with the curli-deficient strain did not elicit robust motor impairment (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The curli-deficient mutant did not display alterations to colonization levels or mucosal association
source: We did not observe curli-dependent alterations to colonization levels or mucosal association, despite detecting csgA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The curli-deficient mutant did not display alterations to lipopolysaccharide potency or structure
source: In addition, the curli-deficient mutant did not display alterations to lipopolysaccharide potency or structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ASO mice colonized with curli-producing bacteria displayed increased αSyn fibril reactivity and detergent-insoluble αSyn in the midbrain
source: ASO mice colonized with curli-producing bacteria displayed increased αSyn fibril reactivity and detergent-insoluble αSyn in the midbrain compared to mice with the ΔcsgBAC strain, despite similar transgene production (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D,F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice colonized with WT E. coli show increased proteinase K-resistant αSyn inclusions in the midbrain
source: Further, mice colonized with WT E. coli show increased proteinase K-resistant αSyn inclusions in the midbrain (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2I), with little alteration to pS129-αSyn in the frontal cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased pS129-αSyn was observed in the proximal large intestine of ASO mice mono-colonized with curli-producing E. coli
source: Additionally, we observed increased pS129-αSyn in the proximal large intestine, and elevated αSyn fibril reactivity in the duodenum and proximal large intestine of ASO mice mono-colonized with curli-producing E. coli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2M–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No decreases in total striatal dopamine, midbrain TH expression, TH+ neurons, or myenteric PGP9.5+ neurons were observed under the colonization conditions and ages assessed
source: Consistent with these prior observations, we do not observe decreases in total striatal dopamine, midbrain TH expression, TH+ neurons, nor myenteric PGP9.5+ neurons, under the colonization conditions and ages assessed, suggesting pathology and motor deficits are independent of dopamine or neuron loss (Figure 1, figure supplement S2Q-S).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mono-colonization of ASO mice with curli-producing E. coli resulted in increased expression of IL-6 and TNFα in brain-derived CD11b+ cells
source: Mono-colonization of ASO mice with curli-producing E. coli resulted in increased expression of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin 6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) in brain-derived CD11b+ cells, and increased cytokine production in the midbrain and striatum (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Iba+ microglia morphologies indicated reduced activation in ASO mice colonized with the curli-deficient strain
source: In addition, Iba+ microglia morphologies indicated reduced activation in ASO mice colonized with the curli-deficient strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Curli-producing E. coli increased cytokine and chemokine production in colonic tissue irrespective of genotype
source: Multiplexed ELISA analysis revealed increased cytokine and chemokine production in colonic tissue of mice mono-colonized with curli-producing E. coli, irrespective of genotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H,J,K), and no noteworthy changes to serum cytokines of ASO mice based on colonization status (Figure 1—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mice harboring a microbiota containing WT E. coli displayed significantly impaired motor and GI performance compared to animals with a complex microbiota plus the curli-deficient strain
source: Mice harboring a microbiota containing WT E. coli displayed significantly impaired motor and GI performance compared to animals with a complex microbiota plus the curli-deficient strain (Figure 2A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Enrichment of curli-producing bacteria resulted in increased αSyn fibril reactivity in the midbrain and elevated pS129-αSyn deposition in the substantia nigra
source: Moreover, enrichment of curli-producing bacteria resulted in increased αSyn fibril reactivity in the midbrain and elevated pS129-αSyn deposition in the SN, without changes to the number of TH+ neurons (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Purified monomeric CsgA accelerated production of αSyn aggregates during in vitro biochemical amyloid assays
source: Purified monomeric CsgA accelerated production of αSyn aggregates during in vitro biochemical amyloid assays (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), even at concentrations below which CsgA self-aggregates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CsgA accelerates αSyn aggregation at concentrations below which CsgA self-aggregates
source: Purified monomeric CsgA accelerated production of αSyn aggregates during in vitro biochemical amyloid assays (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), even at concentrations below which CsgA self-aggregates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: αSyn fibrils purified from CsgA-accelerated reactions maintained an ability to accelerate αSyn amyloidogenesis
source: The αSyn fibrils purified from these reactions maintained an ability to accelerate αSyn amyloidogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), suggesting that CsgA-induced αSyn aggregates are propagation-competent, similar to other amyloids (Spires-Jones et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No direct interaction was detected between purified CsgA and αSyn monomers by surface plasmon resonance
source: Surprisingly, we could not detect a direct interaction between purified CsgA and αSyn monomers by surface plasmon resonance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), perhaps indicating transient interactions or requirements for prior oligomerization of either or both proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tau aggregation was not accelerated by CsgA
source: Unlike αSyn, Tau aggregation was not accelerated by CsgA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Non-amyloidogenic CsgA (SlowGo) did not augment αSyn aggregation in vitro
source: Native amyloid-forming properties of CsgA are required, as a non-amyloidogenic form of CsgA (CsgA:Q49A/N54A/Q139A/N144A; 'SlowGo' Wang and Chapman, 2008) did not augment αSyn aggregation in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Motor performance in ASO mice harboring SlowGo-producing E. coli was less severe compared to mice colonized with WT bacteria
source: Motor performance in ASO mice harboring SlowGo-producing E. coli was less severe in comparison to mice colonized with WT bacteria (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–H), although not to the extent of the ΔcsgBAC strain, qualitatively (see Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intra-intestinal delivery of amyloidogenic CsgA peptide resulted in progressive motor and GI dysfunction in SPF ASO mice
source: Intra-intestinal delivery of amyloidogenic CsgA peptide, but not the mutant peptide, resulted in progressive motor and GI dysfunction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Increased αSyn fibrils were detected in the midbrains of animals injected with amyloidogenic CsgA peptide
source: Furthermore, increased αSyn fibrils were detected in the midbrains of amyloidogenic peptide-injected animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: EGCG physically inhibits amyloid formation, including αSyn aggregation
source: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) is a plant-derived, dietary polyphenol that physically inhibits amyloid formation, including αSyn aggregation (Bieschke et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EGCG blocks CsgA amyloidogenesis and represses csgA transcript expression in E. coli
source: EGCG is also capable of blocking CsgA amyloidogenesis and represses csgA transcript expression in E. coli through activation of specific stress response pathways within the bacterial cell (Serra et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EGCG treatment did not impair E. coli growth in culture but significantly reduced biofilm formation
source: We reveal here that EGCG treatment did not impair E. coli growth in culture, but significantly reduced biofilm formation, a process dependent on the production and assembly of curli (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) (Tursi and Tükel, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGCG inhibited CsgA-accelerated αSyn amyloid formation during in vitro biochemical aggregation assays
source: Additionally, EGCG also inhibited CsgA-accelerated αSyn amyloid formation during in vitro biochemical aggregation assays (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: EGCG remains largely gut-restricted in rodents and humans and is not readily bioavailable in circulation or brain tissues following oral administration
source: Notably, EGCG remains largely gut-restricted in rodents and humans and is not readily bioavailable in circulation or brain tissues following oral administration (Lambert et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2007; Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior pharmacokinetic studies.

claim: Oral treatment of WT E. coli mono-colonized ASO mice with EGCG did not affect fecal E. coli abundance but resulted in decreased csgA production
source: Oral treatment of wild-type E. coli mono-colonized ASO mice with EGCG did not affect fecal E. coli abundance, but resulted in decreased csgA production (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGCG improved both motor and GI defects exacerbated by curli-producing E. coli in ASO mice
source: Assessment of motor performance revealed that EGCG improved both motor and GI defects exacerbated by curli-producing E. coli in ASO mice (Figure 4C–I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oral EGCG administration reduced αSyn aggregation and pS129-αSyn deposition in both the striatum and midbrain
source: In addition, oral EGCG administration reduced αSyn aggregation and pS129-αSyn deposition in both the striatum and midbrain (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microglia morphological changes were limited in EGCG-treated mice
source: Furthermore, microglia morphological changes were limited in EGCG-treated mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O–R).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGCG has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities that may contribute to the rescue of CsgA-accelerated, αSyn-dependent pathophysiology
source: In addition to its ability to directly inhibit aggregation of bacterial and host-derived amyloids, EGCG has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities (Li et al., 2004) that may also contribute to the rescue of CsgA-accelerated, αSyn-dependent pathophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Curli production in the gut of non-susceptible mice does not impair motor performance at the timepoints examined
source: Curli production in the gut of non-susceptible mice does not impair motor performance at the timepoints examined, suggesting that this microbial trigger is not sufficient, but rather requires additional predisposing factors to promote disease outcomes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Inhibiting amyloid formation in the gut correlates with improvements in curli-induced behaviors and pathology
source: Further, inhibiting amyloid formation in the gut correlates with improvements in curli-induced behaviors and pathology.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EGCG treatment experiments.

claim: Aggregates of both CsgA and αSyn are capable of signaling through Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) leading to increased inflammatory responses
source: Aggregates of both CsgA and αSyn are capable of signaling through the innate immune receptor Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) leading to increased inflammatory responses (Tükel et al., 2009; Poewe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibiting TLR2 in αSyn-based mouse models leads to improved pathology and motor outcomes
source: In fact, inhibiting TLR2 in αSyn-based mouse models leads to improved pathology and motor outcomes (Kim et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Synucleinopathy is linked to marked changes to the structure of the microbiome
source: Synucleinopathy is linked to marked changes to the structure of the microbiome.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Numerous studies have reported microbiome differences in persons with Parkinson's disease compared to unaffected individuals
source: Numerous studies have reported microbiome differences in persons with PD compared to unaffected individuals (Hasegawa et al., 2015; Keshavarzian et al., 2015; Scheperjans et al., 2015; Unger et al., 2016; Bedarf et al., 2017; Hill-Burns et al., 2017; Hopfner et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Barichella et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2018); however, examination of the gut microbiome during other synucleinopathies, such as MSA or LBD are still in their infancy (Engen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Some reports have identified the family Enterobacteriaceae as enriched in Parkinson's disease compared to unaffected individuals
source: Some reports have identified the family Enterobacteriaceae as enriched in PD compared to unaffected individuals (Unger et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Barichella et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Enrichment of Enterobacteriaceae is positively associated with worsened motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease
source: In those studies which performed correlation analysis between disease severity and microbiome composition, enrichment of Enterobacteriaceae is observed to be positively associated with worsened motor symptoms (Scheperjans et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Transplant of fecal microbiomes from Parkinson's disease patients into ASO mice results in greater motor deficits than microbiomes from healthy controls
source: In experimental models, however, transplant of fecal microbiomes from PD patients into ASO mice results in greater motor deficits than microbiomes from healthy controls (Sampson et al., 2016), suggesting functional consequences to changes in gut microbial composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Enrichment of Proteus mirabilis or intestinal administration of its purified LPS impairs the dopaminergic system of mice and increases susceptibility to neurotoxins
source: For instance, enrichment of the gut bacterium Proteus mirabilis, or intestinal administration of its purified LPS, impairs the dopaminergic system of mice and increases susceptibility to neurotoxins (Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Infection with Gram-negative bacteria including Citrobacter sp. can trigger pathological processes leading to neurodegenerative immune responses in the brain and loss of midbrain dopamine production
source: Infection with Gram-negative bacteria, including Citrobacter sp. (a taxonomic relative of E. coli), can trigger a pathological process leading to neurodegenerative immune responses in the brain and loss of midbrain dopamine production in a PD-relevant mouse model (Matheoud et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Specific microbiome-derived metabolites promote microglia maturation
source: In addition, specific microbiome-derived metabolites promote microglia maturation (Erny et al., 2015) and enhance αSyn-dependent pathology in germ-free mice (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Specific microbial metabolites or fecal microbiome transplants may provide protection from neurodegenerative insults
source: Conversely, specific microbial metabolites (Blacher et al., 2019) or fecal microbiome transplants (Sun et al., 2018) may provide protection from neurodegenerative insults.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Pseudomonas sp. functional amyloid FapC may accelerate αSyn aggregation in vitro
source: For example, the Pseudomonas sp. functional amyloid, FapC, may also accelerate αSyn aggregation in vitro (Christensen et al., 2019), and bacterial chaperones of CsgA modulate αSyn amyloidogenesis (Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CsgA accelerates amyloid β aggregation in vitro
source: More broadly, CsgA is observed to accelerate amyloid β aggregation in vitro (Hartman et al., 2013; Perov et al., 2019), as well as the disease-associated amyloids, islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) and semen enhancer of viral infection (SEVI) in vitro (Hartman et al., 2013), and serum amyloid A in mice (Lundmark et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CsgA accelerates islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) and semen enhancer of viral infection (SEVI) aggregation in vitro
source: More broadly, CsgA is observed to accelerate amyloid β aggregation in vitro (Hartman et al., 2013; Perov et al., 2019), as well as the disease-associated amyloids, islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) and semen enhancer of viral infection (SEVI) in vitro (Hartman et al., 2013), and serum amyloid A in mice (Lundmark et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CsgA accelerates serum amyloid A aggregation in mice
source: More broadly, CsgA is observed to accelerate amyloid β aggregation in vitro (Hartman et al., 2013; Perov et al., 2019), as well as the disease-associated amyloids, islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) and semen enhancer of viral infection (SEVI) in vitro (Hartman et al., 2013), and serum amyloid A in mice (Lundmark et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Gut bacteria may modulate amyloid-driven diseases including synucleinopathy, Alzheimer's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
source: Emerging evidence in diverse animal models suggests that gut bacteria may modulate amyloid-driven diseases, not only in synucleinopathy as we and others describe, but Alzheimer's disease (Harach et al., 2017; Dodiya et al., 2019) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) as well (Blacher et al., 2019), providing justification for future human studies and revealing possible new targets for interventions that may prevent, slow, or halt amyloid formation and neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents a broader conclusion.

claim: Thy1-αSyn mice were generated on a BDF1 background through breeding female BDF1 background Thy1-αSyn mice to male BDF1 offspring
source: Male wild-type and Thy1-αSyn mice (Line 61, with permission from University of California, San Diego) were generated as described previously (Rockenstein et al., 2002; Chesselet et al., 2012; Sampson et al., 2016), through breeding female BDF1 background Thy1-αSyn mice to male BDF1 offspring generated via crossing female C57BL/6 with DBA/2 males (Charles River, Hollister, CA), and refreshing breeding pairs ~ 6 months.
evidence: This describes the methods used to generate the mouse model.

claim: Germ-free Thy1-αSyn breeding pairs were generated via caesarian section and cross-fostered by GF Swiss-Webster dams
source: Germ-free (GF) Thy1-αSyn breeding pairs were generated via caesarian section and cross-fostered by GF Swiss-Webster dams.
evidence: This describes the methods used to generate germ-free mice.

claim: Mono-colonized animals received ~10^8 cfu of the indicated bacterial strains at 5-6 weeks of age
source: Mono-colonized animals received ~108 cfu of the indicated bacterial strains in ~100 μL sodium bicarbonate buffer (5% w/v) at 5–6 weeks of age.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for bacterial colonization.

claim: Human microbiome colonized animals received fecal extract from a previously sampled healthy human donor
source: Human microbiome colonized animals received ~100 μL 0.1 g/mL fecal extract from previously sampled healthy human donor (ENA Accession: PRJEB17694; Sample #: 10483.donor2.HC; MMA_008 [Sampson et al., 2016], California Institute of Technology's Institutional Review Board #15–0568- exempt), at 5–6 weeks of age.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for human microbiome transplantation.

claim: EGCG was administered at 200 μg/mL in drinking water ad libitum beginning at 5-6 weeks of age
source: For epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) treatment, animals received filter-sterilized EGCG (Sigma Aldrich) at 200 μg/mL in drinking water ad libitum beginning at 5–6 weeks of age.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for EGCG treatment.
